Russian has no perfect tenses: an action that started earlier and is still going on is simply the present, "я работаю". The English "I've been working" has no separate form here — the duration is carried by the words that follow, not by the verb.

"Один и тот же" is a fixed three-word phrase for "the same", and both parts decline: here the prepositional after "в" gives "в одной и той же". Saying "в тот же команде" would leave the agreement broken.
"Уже" plus the plain accusative expresses duration up to now: "уже три года". There is no preposition at all, so the English "for" has nothing to translate into.
"В последнее время" is a fixed phrase in the prepositional case, literally "in the last time", meaning "recently". It is one of the very few time expressions that keeps "в".
The past of "начать", masculine. Russian marks the speaker's gender here, not the person: a woman would say "начала".

After "начал" the second verb stays in the infinitive: "начал чувствовать". And where English says "to feel stuck" with an adjective, Russian opens a subordinate clause with "что" and a full verb — there is no way to attach a participle directly.
The subject in the nominative. Russian often drops the possessive where English needs one: "руководитель" alone is understood as "my manager".
"Предложить" is perfective, a single completed act. "Короткий курс" is the accusative of an inanimate masculine noun, so neither word changes its ending.
"На прошлой неделе" takes "на", not "в" — weeks are the exception. "Записался" carries the particle "-ся", which makes it "signed myself up".
In an "если" clause Russian does use the future, unlike English: "если всё пойдёт хорошо". A present tense here would change the meaning to a repeated condition.
"Возможно" is set off by commas and can be dropped without breaking the sentence — that is exactly why it takes them. "Подам" is a perfective future: no auxiliary word is needed.
"Подать заявку на что-то" takes "на" plus the accusative: "на другую должность". Both words are feminine accusative, so both change their endings.
"Переехать" is perfective and specifically means moving house. The plural past "переехали" agrees with "мы" in number, with no marking for person.
Direction with "в" plus the accusative: "новая квартира" becomes "в новую квартиру". With the prepositional, "в новой квартире", it would mean already living there.
Months take "в" plus the prepositional: "апрель" becomes "в апреле".
The subject in the nominative. "Дом" here means the building, not the home — that meaning belongs to the adverb "дома".
A full adjective as predicate, with no verb: the present tense of "быть" is not used in Russian. "Старый" agrees with the masculine "дом".
"Что-то" is an indefinite pronoun, "something", and takes a singular verb. "Ломается" has "-ся", so things break by themselves. "Довольно часто" means "quite often".
Months take "в" plus the prepositional: "прошлый месяц" becomes "в прошлом месяце".
"Отопление" is a neuter noun in the nominative, the subject of what follows. Russian has no article, so nothing marks it as "the heating".
The imperfective past for a state that lasted: "не работало", neuter to agree with "отопление". "Целую неделю" is the accusative of duration, with no preposition.
"Хозяин квартиры" links two nouns with the genitive, "квартиры", where English uses a single word "landlord". This genitive link is Russian's standard way of joining nouns.
"В итоге" means "in the end". "Починил" is perfective, so the repair was completed; "чинил" would say he was working on it without saying he finished.
"Занять" is perfective, "to take up time". "Слишком много времени" puts the noun in the genitive after "много" — a quantity word always demands it.
The present tense with no perfect: "я учу испанский" covers "I have been learning". "Учить" means to study a subject; "изучать" is its more formal partner.
"Примерно" means "about". The duration goes in the plain accusative with no preposition: "год".
"В основном" is a fixed phrase meaning "mostly". Russian says "в телефоне", inside the phone, where English says "on my phone" — the preposition is genuinely different.
After "мочь" the verb stays in the infinitive: "могу читать". "Читать" is imperfective, describing the ability rather than one completed act.
"Меню" is indeclinable and neuter, so it never changes. "Статьи" is the accusative plural, identical to the nominative for inanimate nouns, with the adjective agreeing.
"Без" always takes the genitive: "особые сложности" becomes "особых сложностей". Note that the genitive plural of this noun has no ending of its own.
An infinitive used as the subject: "говорить" here means "speaking". Russian has no gerund for this, so the infinitive does the job.
"Вот что" points forward and adds emphasis, roughly "that is what". "Трудно" is a neuter short form used impersonally, with no verb at all.
"Особенно" means "especially". "По телефону" uses "по" plus the dative — a fixed way of saying "by phone", not translatable preposition by preposition.
The instrumental with no preposition for a season: "следующим летом", like "весной" and "вечером". Both words take instrumental endings.
"Хотел бы" is the conditional, formed with the past tense plus the particle "бы". It softens "хочу" exactly as English "would like" softens "want".
"Провести" is perfective, "to spend time". "Две недели" is the accusative of duration, and after "две" the noun takes the genitive singular. The city takes "в" plus the prepositional: "в Валенсии".
"Наш" agrees with the masculine "рейс", and the whole phrase is the object of the next verb, though its form does not change.
Russian uses a subjectless plural verb where English uses the passive: "задержали" means "they delayed it", with no "they" named. "Рейс" is the accusative object, identical to the nominative.
"На" plus the accusative expresses the size of a difference: "на четыре часа". After "четыре" the noun takes the genitive singular, "часа".
"Никто" is a negative pronoun, and Russian requires the verb to be negated as well: "никто не смог". This double negation is compulsory, the exact opposite of the English rule.
"На стойке" uses "на" plus the prepositional for a service point. The choice between "в" and "на" here is fixed by usage and simply has to be learned.
"Смог" is the perfective past of "мочь", and the negation "не" stands before it, matching "никто". After it the infinitive: "объяснить почему".
"В итоге" again, "in the end".
Another subjectless plural: "нам выдали" is "they gave us". The recipient goes into the dative, "нам", and the thing given into the accusative.
"Талон на бутерброд" uses "на" plus the accusative for what the voucher is for. Russian has no articles, so nothing marks either noun as definite.
"Решить" is perfective, the decision made once. The masculine past again depends on the speaker's gender.
After "решил" the verb stays in the infinitive: "лететь". "Другой авиакомпанией" is in the instrumental — the case Russian uses for the means of doing something.
"В следующий раз" takes "в" plus the accusative, unlike English "next time", which needs no preposition at all.
"Когда-то" means "at one time, once". The imperfective past "играл" describes a lasting habit, which is how Russian expresses English "used to play" — there is no separate construction for it.
Playing an instrument uses "на" plus the prepositional: "на гитаре", "на пианино". Playing a game would use "в" plus the accusative: "в футбол".
"Учиться" has "-ся" and means to be a student. "В школе" uses "в" plus the prepositional.
"Бросить" is perfective, "to give up". "Это" is the accusative object and refers back to playing the guitar.
After "начал" the verb stays in the infinitive: "начал работать", imperfective, because the work is a continuing state.
"Потом" means "afterwards". "Жалел" is imperfective past: the regret lasted rather than happening once.
"Мой друг" in the nominative as the subject. Russian says "друг" for a close friend; a mere acquaintance would be "знакомый".

"Одолжить" takes the recipient in the dative, "мне", and the thing in the accusative. "Свою старую" is a feminine adjective standing alone for "his old guitar" — Russian needs no equivalent of English "one".
Months with "в" plus the prepositional: "январь" becomes "в январе".
"Теперь" contrasts the present with an earlier state, whereas "сейчас" would mean "at this very moment".
"Заниматься" always takes the instrumental when it has an object, but here it stands alone and means "to practise, to study".
"По" plus the accusative distributes a quantity: "по двадцать минут" means twenty minutes each time. "Каждый вечер" is the accusative of a repeated time, with no preposition.
"Моя" agrees with the feminine "сестра", and the phrase is the subject, so it stays in the nominative.
"Только что" means "just now" and goes with a perfective past. Russian has no perfect tense, so the adverb carries all the meaning that English puts into "has just".
"Первый курс университета" links two nouns with the genitive: "университета". And "курс" means an academic year, not a course of lectures — that would be "курс лекций".
"Изучает" is imperfective present, for an ongoing course of study. Russian makes no distinction between "she studies" and "she is studying".
"Что-то связанное с данными" uses a participle plus "с" with the instrumental. "Данные" is plural only, and its instrumental is "данными".
"Чего" is the genitive of "что", required because the verb is negated: after a negative verb the object often shifts from accusative to genitive. "Толком" means "properly, really".
"Каждый раз, когда" is the standard rendering of English "whenever", and the comma before "когда" is compulsory.
"Объяснять" takes the thing in the accusative and the person in the dative, so "мне" could be added freely. Here the object is left out because it is obvious.
"Терпеливо" is an adverb formed from "терпеливый". "Очень" intensifies it and stands directly before.
"По-прежнему" means "still, as before" and is written with a hyphen. It is more emphatic than a plain "ещё".
"Ничего не понимаю" has the compulsory double negation again: "ничего" and "не" must both be present. "Ничего" is the genitive form used after a negated verb.
"Всё равно" means "anyway, all the same". "Гордиться" always takes the instrumental: "ею", the instrumental of "она".
"Должны были" plus the infinitive means an obligation that existed in the past; like English "were supposed to", it hints that it did not happen. "Запустить" is perfective.
The accusative of an inanimate masculine noun, unchanged in form: "новый сайт".
Months with "в" plus the prepositional: "июнь" becomes "в июне".
"Потом" means "then, after that". "Дизайнер" is the subject in the nominative.
"Уйти из" plus the genitive means leaving an organisation: "из компании". The pair "в" and "из" work together, so a place you go "в" you leave "из".

"Всё" here means "everything" and takes a singular verb. "Встало" is a perfective past of "встать" used figuratively, "came to a halt". "На месяц" uses "на" plus the accusative for an intended period.
"Наконец" means "finally" and needs no commas in this position.
"Выкатить" is a colloquial perfective for releasing a product. "Его" is the accusative of "он", referring to the site.
Days of the week take "в" plus the accusative: "в прошлый четверг", with the day in lower case.
"Пока что" means "so far, for now". Russian has no perfect tense to pair it with, so the plain past does the work.
"Никто не пожаловался" is the compulsory double negation again. "Пожаловаться" is perfective and takes "на" plus the accusative when the complaint has an object.
"Похоже на" plus the accusative means "looks like". "Уже" here means "already" and adds the sense that this is more than expected.
"Стараться" is imperfective, an effort that goes on. It is followed by an infinitive with nothing in between.
"Вести бюджет" is the fixed collocation, literally "to lead a budget". "Бюджет" is the accusative of an inanimate masculine noun, unchanged.
"Получается" is an impersonal verb with "-ся": there is no subject at all, and the sentence means "it does not work out well". "Не очень" is a mild understatement.
The subject in the nominative. Russian has no article, so nothing marks "проблема" as "the problem".
"Не в крупных тратах" uses "в" plus the prepositional after the negation. The construction "не в чём-то, а в чём-то" is fixed and both halves must keep the same case.
"А" contrasts with the negated half and is not the same as "и" or "но". "В мелких" keeps the prepositional to match "в крупных тратах" — the noun is dropped but the case is not.
The nominative as subject. "Кофе" is indeclinable, so it looks the same everywhere.
"Такси" is also indeclinable and neuter: it has no plural ending, and the verb after it comes from the pair "кофе и такси".
"Набегают" is a figurative use of "набегать", "to add up". After "чем" comes a full clause: "чем кажется", where "кажется" is impersonal.
"В этом месяце" takes "в" plus the prepositional, like "в прошлом месяце".
The imperfective present "записываю" covers a habit that is still going on. Russian has no perfect, so the month being unfinished is not marked by the verb.
"Каждый платёж" is the accusative object, unchanged in form. "Каждый" always takes a singular noun.
"Плохо" is an adverb and goes before the verb. "Сплю" is the first person of the irregular "спать".

In an "если" clause about a repeated condition Russian uses the present. "Смотреть в" plus the accusative is how Russian talks about staring into a screen; "смотреть на" would mean looking at it from outside.
"Поздно вечером" combines an adverb with the instrumental of time. Neither part takes a preposition.
"Пробовать" is imperfective, an attempt made more than once. Its perfective partner "попробовать" would point to one single try.
After "пробовал" the verb stays in the infinitive, and the imperfective "оставлять" says it was a repeated arrangement, not one act.
"На кухне" takes "на", not "в" — one of the fixed choices Russian makes for certain places, alongside "на работе" and "на почте".
"Это" refers back to the whole arrangement. "Работает" is used figuratively for "it works", exactly as in English.
"Но только" restricts what follows. "Только" stands directly before the part it limits.
"Действительно" means "really, in fact". "Так делаю" is literally "do it that way": "так" replaces the whole action.
The nominative plural as the subject, with no article: "привычки" means habits in general.
"Гораздо" intensifies a comparative, like English "much". "Легче" is the comparative of "лёгкий", formed with "-е" and a consonant change.

After "чем" the form matches what came before: two infinitives, "запланировать" and "соблюдать". Note that the first is perfective and the second imperfective, and that difference is deliberate: planning happens once, keeping goes on.
"Моя старая машина" is the subject in the nominative, with both the possessive and the adjective agreeing in the feminine.
"Наконец" means "finally" and takes no commas here.
"Умерла" is a perfective past agreeing with the feminine "машина". Using it about a car is a live metaphor in Russian, as in English. "В феврале" is "в" plus the prepositional.
"Вместо того чтобы" is a fixed conjunction followed by an infinitive: "покупать новую". The imperfective says the buying is thought of as a process, not a single act.
"Решить" is perfective, a decision made once.
After "решил" comes the infinitive "попробовать". "Электричка" is a suburban commuter train specifically, not any train — that would be "поезд".
"Дорога" here means the journey rather than the road. The subject in the nominative.
"Занимает" is imperfective present, for something that is regularly true. "Больше времени" puts the noun in the genitive after "больше", as quantity words always do.
"В пути" is a fixed prepositional phrase, "on the way", from the noun "путь". "Можно" is impersonal and takes an infinitive with no subject at all.
"Не думаю" carries the negation in the main clause, exactly as English does. The subject "я" can be dropped here, and often is.
"Вернусь" is a perfective future with the particle "-сь". No auxiliary word is needed for the future.
"Вернуться к" plus the dative: "к вождению". "Вождение" is a verbal noun, and Russian uses it where English uses the gerund "driving".
